title: Bend a 45 degree offset in 1/8 in copper tube on a Swagelok hand tube bender clamped in a vise
instruction: Use the hand bender to bend a 45 degree offset at the tube's two marks, turn the roll support back to 0, and let go.
context: Heating, air conditioning and refrigeration mechanics (O*NET 49-9021.00, 397,450 US workers; "bend pipe or tubing") and plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (47-2152.00, 510,600; together about 908,000) bend small tube by hand every day: 1/8 in copper is the stock size of refrigeration capillary and gauge sensing lines and small instrument impulse lines, and an offset steps such a line sideways round a fitting or bracket. Swagelok's bender manual gives the layout: the two bend marks lie O x 1.414 apart for a 45 degree offset (MS-13-43, p.11), and the second bend is a reverse bend, the tube turned so its reference mark lies on the other side of the latch (p.18). The work is two opposite bends at measured marks, each pulled against the tube's own stiffness; between them the tube is eased under its latch, slid to the second mark and turned half a turn about its axis. Measured is the finished part, still in the bender: the offset between the straight ends and whether they run parallel.
setup: A Swagelok MS-HTB-2 hand tube bender (1/8 in OD tube, 9/16 in = 14.3 mm bend radius; manual MS-13-43) is clamped by its vise clamp block in a 3 in vise on the table, bend plane horizontal, the bender die's axis at (26, -8) cm and the tube's centre line 7.5 cm above the table in the die's groove. The bend radius and tube size are the maker's; the bender's other sizes are estimates from the manual's photographs. The die's groove has lips 3 mm thick above and below the tube and a straight groove 3 cm long continues it on the latch side. The long handle (2.2 cm across, 4 to 26 cm from the die axis, dark-blue grip from 16 cm) points along -20 degrees 3.5 cm below the tube's plane; it is clamped and never touched. The roll support turns about the die axis under the die. The short handle hangs on a clevis pin on it, 3.5 cm below the tube's plane, its dark-blue cushion grip 2.2 cm across from 16 to 26 cm from the die axis; it starts along 70 degrees (90 degrees from the long handle) and turns anticlockwise seen from above. It carries two steel roll dies 10 mm across on axles up to the tube's plane, the first resting on the tube where it leaves the die, the second 2.2 cm further along (real dies are grooved; simulated, each is a plain 10 x 8 mm cylinder with a 2 mm disc above it that reaches 2.4 mm over the tube, 1.2 mm clear of it). Swung up and away about its clevis (to a stop at 45 degrees) the short handle lifts the roll dies off the tube; lowered, the link holds them on it. The tube latch is a steel keeper plate 12 mm long beside the tube on the latch side, 1.2 to 2.4 cm from where the tube leaves the die, with a lip resting on the tube's top; it is hinged on a pin 3 cm along, across the tube, so it lifts in its own plane (to 50 degrees). A red post 8 x 8 mm stands 1.8 cm above the tube on it, 1.6 to 2.4 cm along: pushed along the tube toward the pin it lifts the keeper, which stays where it is put (the spring washer on its screw); let down, it rests on the tube and holds it lightly; pressed down firmly it clamps it. Degree marks 0 to 90 every 15 degrees from the start line are on the name plate under the die; the roll support carries a red 0. The tube is 1/8 in (3.18 mm) OD x 0.030 in (0.76 mm) wall seamless soft-annealed copper, ASTM B280, UNS C12200, 30 cm long, 16 g, with two black marks 7.07 cm apart centred on its length (5.0 cm x 1.414) and a yellow direction mark 1 cm from end A. At the start it lies straight in the groove, the latch resting on it, with mark A, the one nearer end A, at the roll support's 45 degree mark (its 45 degree wrap centred on the mark, 5.6 mm past where the tube leaves the die), end A on the roll dies' side pointing along 160 degrees, and the roll dies resting on it: the state after the manual's set-up steps 1 to 7 (pp.12-14). Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x (away from the robot) and the table's centre line in y (+y toward the left arm), angles anticlockwise from +x seen from above. The screenshot shows the start.
scoring: Read at the end of the run. A hand is a gripper's fingertip midpoint; the tube is let go only with both hands 6 cm or more from every part of it. A bend counts only if it goes round the die and the bender made it: on the real tube its inside fits the bender's 9/16 in (14.3 mm) radius within 4 mm (radius gauge) and the video shows it formed by turning the short handle with the roll dies on the tube; in the simulation it is spread over 3 or more hinges carrying 1 degree or more, its radius (bent length over angle) is 10 to 18 mm, and at most a quarter of it (or 5 degrees) was made with the roll support still or the roll dies up. 0 for good if a bend passes 55 degrees, or if the two bends go the same way (a U, not an offset). 0 if the tube isn't let go. A bend sits at its mark if its vertex point lies within 3.5 mm of the mark's centre, along the tube: lay a straightedge along each of the bend's two straight lengths and mark where their centre lines meet (the bend's vertex, the maker's manual's (MS-13-43) measuring point); the point of the tube's centre line nearest the vertex, the bend's middle, is measured from the mark with a ruler (in the simulation, the same point from the tube's shape). 3.5 mm is the sum of half the 2 mm mark's width, 1 mm reading the ruler and the manual's 1.6 mm gain for this tube at 45 degrees; it keeps the mark on the 11.2 mm arc. Otherwise, angles read after springback with a protractor between the straight lengths: 0.25 for one counted bend at 45 +/- 4 degrees that sits at its mark (a bend off its mark is not a correct bend); 0.5 for both; 0.75 with the two ends also parallel within 3 degrees and 5.0 +/- 0.4 cm apart, centreline to centreline (tape), all read on the tube where it sits latched in the bender; 0.9 with the roll support also back at its 0 mark within 5 degrees (its red 0 against the name plate's marks); 1.0 with the tube also at rest (every part moving under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s, averaged over each 0.05 s step; in a real trial, still on the video) for the last 1 s. The 5.0 cm offset follows from the formula; the tolerances are this task's own, not a maker's or an industry limit.
reset_notes: A bent tube can't be straightened, so every trial takes a fresh 30 cm length cut from the coil, straightened by hand along a straightedge, marked 360 degrees round with a fine marker at the two marks 7.07 cm apart (centred on its length) and with a direction mark 1 cm from end A. Set the bender as the screenshot shows: roll support at 0, tube latched with mark A at the roll support's 45 degree mark, roll dies resting on the tube, short handle down at the start. After scoring, lift the latch and take the finished tube out by hand.
fidelity: Real 1/8 in tube at real force: the arms push 3-5 N (3/8 in steel would need about 100 N). Tube: round 3.18 mm links, 16 g, hinged every 2.5 mm within 2.5 cm of each mark; each hinge has the tube's E I and yields at 0.38 N m (Z_p 4.6 mm3 x 84 MPa, textbook copper). Our estimates: bender sizes; latch light hold 0.05 N m, firm 0.12 N m, 0.03 N m friction off its seat; roll support friction 0.20 N m; link a detent; roll dies plain cylinders with an upper lip (real ones grooved).
